title: Acute Deterioration & Rescue
html:
Physiological adaptation asks the RN to manage acute, chronic, and life-threatening conditions. In a deteriorating client, act on the immediate threat while continuing focused assessment and mobilizing help.

Use a rapid priority frame

  • Airway obstruction, inadequate breathing, poor perfusion, and acute neurologic change demand immediate attention.
  • Call for the level of help the situation requires; do not leave an unstable client to search for equipment or a provider.
  • Begin nursing actions within scope and the emergency plan while the team responds.
Intervene, then reassess
Every rescue action needs a response check. Improvement, no change, and worsening each determine the next step.

Remove a harmful source

When a treatment may be causing an acute reaction, stop or pause the suspected source when indicated, maintain safety, assess airway and circulation, and follow the emergency protocol. Preserve needed access or equipment according to the situation.

Think beyond the first number

A normal single vital sign does not erase altered mentation, poor urine output, new work of breathing, or weak perfusion. Integrate the full picture and escalate early.

Learning goals

Recognize a rescue situation, summon appropriate help, and reassess after an immediate action. These examples introduce emergency recognition; they do not confer BLS certification or replace supervised resuscitation training.

Unresponsive adult: recognize arrest

Check scene safety and responsiveness, summon help, activate the emergency response system, and obtain an AED. A healthcare professional checks breathing and pulse together for no more than 10 seconds. If there is no normal breathing (only gasping) and no definite pulse, begin CPR, starting with compressions, and use the AED as soon as available. Follow current BLS training and prompts, minimizing interruptions. Gasping is not normal breathing. When a pulse is definitely present but breathing is absent or inadequate, provide ventilation and reassessment according to the BLS algorithm.

New neurologic change

Sudden facial asymmetry, unilateral weakness, or speech difficulty requires immediate stroke-pathway activation. Record the last-known-well time and assess glucose promptly per protocol without delaying escalation. Do not offer food, drink, or oral medication while swallowing safety is uncertain. Improvement of a symptom does not justify canceling urgent assessment.

Suspected transfusion reaction

New chills, back pain, dyspnea, or hypotension during blood administration can signal a serious reaction. Stop the transfusion, assess airway, breathing, circulation and vital signs, summon help as needed, and notify the provider and transfusion service. Maintain IV access using the appropriate new tubing/access per policy; do not flush residual blood from the existing line into the client. Retain the blood bag and administration set for investigation. Do not restart a suspected serious reaction transfusion on your own.

Escalate suspected sepsis

Infection with new confusion, hypotension, tachypnea, or poor perfusion needs immediate assessment and the local sepsis pathway. A screening score supports recognition but does not replace judgment. Prepare to carry out time-critical ordered care, continue monitoring, and report deterioration despite initial treatment.

Closed-loop teamwork

State the task, identify who will perform it, and confirm completion. Record key times once immediate help is underway. After each action, reassess breathing, perfusion, and responsiveness; do not regard one improved number as full recovery.

Sources for review

  • AHA: 2025 CPR and ECC guidelines
  • Lifeblood: Suspected transfusion reactions

Original educational synthesis. Local protocols and qualified faculty guide clinical application.
